prize_parts.citation: for discoveries of GLP-1 as an incretin hormone and of its active forms and actions, which made possible incretin-based therapy of type 2 diabetes and obesity

statement.case_for: B036 is the only candidate that all six of us placed first, and I do not rest on that alone. The chain from proglucagon processing and the identification of the active GLP-1(7-36) peptide, through human incretin physiology and the intestinotrophic and cardiometabolic biology, to long-acting agonists is unusually complete. Independent randomized outcome trials show effects on glycaemia, weight, cardiovascular and renal outcomes, and the interpretation has been stable for years. From the clinic I see how this has changed management of a very large patient population. A prize built on the physiology (Holst, Mojsov, Drucker) credits the discovery of the hormone's biology and keeps the therapeutic consequence in the citation.
statement.case_against: The attribution is the weak point. Four names are credited but only three can be honoured, Habener is outside the supplied credit, and my recollection of Mojsov's priority relative to others is unverified. If the committee thinks the decisive achievement is the engineered drugs, my configuration leaves out Knudsen and rewards the physiology rather than the medicine. There is also a risk that a physiology-centred trio looks like it under-credits industrial drug development that actually reached patients.

responses.point: Linnarsson ranks B036 first but proposes Drucker, Holst and Knudsen, treating the long-acting agonists as the key translational step in place of Mojsov.
responses.response: I take the argument seriously: liraglutide and semaglutide are what patients receive. But the Nobel criterion is the discovery. Knudsen's work builds on the identification of the active peptide and its biology, and that peptide work is the part nobody else could have supplied. I would credit Mojsov over Knudsen on that basis. I concede the choice is not clear-cut. If our later discussion finds that Mojsov's priority claim cannot be supported on the evidence in the file, I would move to Knudsen rather than leave the third slot to a contested name.

responses.point: Sandberg also puts B036 first with Knudsen as the translation representative and calls Mojsov's contribution real but contested; he ranks optogenetics (B042) second.
responses.response: I agree that Mojsov's credit is contested and that we should say so openly. Where I differ is on the remedy: dropping her to represent translation changes the prize from a discovery prize to a development prize, and leaves the physiological story with two people. On optogenetics I agree it is a mature, broadly validated tool, but six credited names and a methods-versus-discovery question make it a harder configuration than B036, so I keep it as an alternative and not as a co-recipient.

responses.point: Wahren-Herlenius ranks TNF blockade (B031) second, as a clean bench-to-bedside discovery with a natural two-person configuration (Feldmann and Maini), and mature.
responses.response: B031 is a strong, mature candidate and the two-person attribution is tidier than B036. My reservation is that the field has other contributors to TNF biology and antibody engineering whose claims are not resolved in the supplied credit, and the principle has since been partly absorbed into later cytokine therapies. I would not object to it as a second part of a two-achievement prize, but I did not rank it in my top eight on opening, and I have not seen an argument that moves it above the unfolded protein response or optogenetics.

responses.point: Perlmann argues for the same physiology trio in B036 and puts B006 (Walter and Mori) second as a clean conceptual discovery.
responses.response: We agree on B036 and on B006 as a strong second. My qualification is on B006: clinical impact is still developing, and other groups' work on the PERK and ATF6 arms is not assessed in the file. The fit with the criteria is conceptual, not therapeutic, so I think it works best as an alternative or as a second part, not as a replacement for B036. I note that Perlmann and I have co-authored work, but this does not relate to either candidate.

uncertainties: Whether Mojsov's priority over Knudsen (and Habener, who is not on the credited list) can be sustained from the supplied evidence.
Whether the committee wants to honour the physiology, the drug development, or both, and whether a two-part prize would be better than a single part.
Whether the unfolded protein response or optogenetics belongs in a two-achievement configuration given the three-person limit.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for any shortlisted candidate. I worked with Paul Greengard as a postdoctoral fellow and have co-authored work with Thomas Perlmann, but neither relates to the credited names on the shortlist.
